title: Dry Eye Is a Menopause Symptom Almost Nobody Warns You About
hook: Around half of women in the menopausal transition have dry eye symptoms, and the rate in women over 50 is double that of men. The culprit is usually oil glands in the eyelids, not a shortage of tears.
key_points: Research suggests around half of all women in the menopausal transition years have dry eye symptoms.
Large studies put dry eye in women over 50 at double the rate in men over 50.
The usual cause is failing oil glands in the eyelids — too little oil, or oil too thick to release — so tears evaporate too fast.
Androgens help regulate those glands, which is why declining sex hormones with age and menopause matter.
Screens, contacts, allergies, rosacea, and common drugs like blood pressure medications and antidepressants all contribute.
Treatments range from warm compresses and over-the-counter drops to prescriptions and in-office gland procedures; expect trial and error.
content_html: Hilda Hernandez Nash was driving to work when her eyes suddenly felt gritty. "All of a sudden, I couldn't tolerate my contacts. My eyes just felt like they were sandpaper," she told NPR. Within days they were red, watery, and swollen, and she couldn't tolerate light. She assumed pink eye. What she actually had was dry eye — a condition, her eye doctor explained, that many women meet as they enter perimenopause.
extra_html:
It's far more common than its low profile suggests. Research indicates around half of all women in the menopausal transition years have symptoms, and Johns Hopkins optometrist Lauren Gormley notes that large-scale studies put the rate of dry eye in women over 50 at double the rate in men over 50. The mechanism is less about tear quantity than tear quality: oil glands in the eyelids normally keep tears from evaporating, and when the oil is too scarce, too thick, or can't be released, the tear film breaks down and the eye surface becomes inflamed. Androgens help regulate those glands, so declining sex hormones with age and menopause tip the balance.

Plenty of non-hormonal factors stack on top. Kelly Nichols, dean of optometry at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, points to screens — we blink less when staring at them, so tears spread poorly — plus contact lenses, allergies, rosacea, and common medications including blood pressure drugs and antidepressants.

The reason not to shrug it off is functional: research has shown dry eye affects quality of life, from work performance to reading and driving. "Should you go to the doctor? Yes," Nichols says, "because your eyes shouldn't impact your quality of life." Treatments run from warm compresses and over-the-counter drops through prescription medications to in-office procedures that unclog the eyelid glands, though those can be expensive and are often not covered by insurance. Expect some trial and error before something works.

related.title: Protecting Your Eyes
related.hook: Some of the most serious eye diseases, like glaucoma, steal sight silently with no early symptoms. A regular eye exam is often the only way to catch them in time.

related.title: Menopause: What to Expect

related.title: That Ringing in Your Ears Can Be an Early Warning
related.hook: Hearing loss rarely arrives as silence. It often shows up first as ringing in the ears or a struggle to follow conversation in a noisy room — signs worth heeding early.

flashcards.prompt: What's the most common underlying cause of dry eye described here?

choices.text: Oil glands in the eyelids producing too little or poor-quality oil, so tears evaporate too fast
The tear ducts being physically blocked
Permanent damage to the cornea from sunlight

flashcards.explanation_html: Optometrist Lauren Gormley explains the oil can be too low in volume, too thick, or unable to be released into the tear film — leading to fast evaporation and inflammation of the ocular surface, "which is really what dry eye is."

flashcards.prompt: What links dry eye to menopause?
flashcards.back_html: Androgens help regulate oil production in the eyelid glands. As androgen levels decline with age and menopause, those glands make less oil and lower-quality oil. Around half of women in the menopausal transition report symptoms.

flashcards.prompt: Watery, red eyes rule out dry eye — true or false?

choices.text: False — dry eye can present as gritty, red, watery, swollen, light-sensitive eyes
True — dry eye always means visibly dry eyes with no tearing
True — watering always means an infection

flashcards.explanation_html: The patient in NPR's story first thought she had pink eye: her eyes felt like sandpaper, then turned red, watery and swollen, and she couldn't tolerate light. Dry eye is an inflammation of the ocular surface, not simply an absence of moisture.
